tldr: This review paper summarizes the current state of legged robots stepping into the real world thanks to hardware evolution and breakthroughs in simulation reinforcement learning, systematically laying out future challenges across dexterous motion, autonomy, data, and socioeconomic impacts.
hero_caption: Diagram illustrating the hardware architecture and historical evolution of legged robots. It provides an overview of biological analogies for robot components, the internal structure of quasi-direct drive (QDD) actuators, the shift in control paradigms (from classical control to reinforcement learning), and the recent explosive growth and performance distribution of quadrupedal and humanoid robots.
overview:
Once confined to science fiction and dedicated research cages in laboratories, legged robots (quadrupeds and humanoids) are now being deployed in the real world—from factory inspections and last-mile delivery to disaster zones. Legged mechanisms have carried enormous expectations because they can traverse steps and stairs that wheels cannot, operating directly within environments built for humans. However, formidable obstacles stood in the way, including vulnerability to severe impact shocks, complex whole-body dynamics, and the gap between simulation and the physical world (the Sim-to-Real gap).

This paper unpacks the technological drivers that transformed this landscape. On the hardware side, the widespread adoption of quasi-direct drive (QDD) actuators—combining low gear ratios with high-torque motors—achieved both impact resilience and high-bandwidth, responsive torque control. On the software side, pairing GPU-parallel physics simulators with reinforcement learning (RL) compressed thousands of hours of trial and error. This enabled zero-shot transfer (without fine-tuning on the real system) of robust controllers that do not fall, even on unmapped, rugged terrain.

The authors systematically organize current achievements across six axes: hardware, locomotion, autonomy and representations, data and simulations, real-world applications, and policy and economics. Building on this, they argue that legged robots must transition beyond mere "stable walking" toward "dexterous semantic locomotion" that integrates vision and semantic understanding to handle fragile footholds and manipulate tools, outlining a roadmap toward general Embodied AI.
contributions: Systematizing the evolution of hardware design philosophy—from overcoming low backdrivability to adopting QDD actuators—that underpinned the recent explosion of modern legged robots.

Clarifying the success factors of Sim-to-Real RL in locomotion control, and defining the next-generation challenge of "dexterous semantic locomotion" that integrates visual and semantic understanding.
Comparing classical modular navigation pipelines with unified autonomous architectures leveraging modern foundation models such as VLAs and diffusion models, and outlining open challenges.
Analyzing the impacts of legged robots on industry, the economy, and the labor market, and proposing policy recommendations such as capability-based tiered regulation and data flywheels.

sections.heading: From the lab to the real world: What is happening with legged robots?
sections.summary: Unlike wheeled systems or drones, legged robots combine rough-terrain traversability with high payload capacity and compatibility with human environments. Recently, lower hardware costs and breakthroughs in machine learning have converged, rapidly accelerating real-world deployment and commercial investment beyond academia.
sections.details:
Research on legged robots spans several decades. Starting with 1960s–70s hydraulic heavy-walking machines like the General Electric Walking Truck and pioneering humanoids like WABOT-1 led by Ichiro Kato in Japan, followed by Marc Raibert's pioneering dynamic balance walking, the field evolved toward Honda ASIMO and Boston Dynamics' BigDog and LS3. Back then, however, these systems were exceedingly expensive, fragile, and bound to the lab due to the sheer complexity of classical control algorithms.

The decisive paradigm shift in recent years stems from reliable, low-cost actuators, miniaturized sensors, improved on-board computing, and, crucially, the spread of open-source designs. Combined with advances in parallel GPU simulation and reinforcement learning (RL), robots have acquired the agility to run through diverse environments without years of manual control-gain tuning.

This review is more than a technical survey. Against the backdrop of commercialized quadrupedal robots and the humanoid boom accelerating through the mid-2020s, it aims to deliver an end-to-end perspective covering technological milestones, limitations, practical applications, and broad socioeconomic effects including labor markets and policy regulation.

sections.heading: Reinventing muscle and skeleton: Why high-torque backdrivable actuators matter
sections.summary: Legged robot hardware must withstand massive impact loads at touchdown (up to 3 times body weight) while executing high-bandwidth torque control. After journeying through heavy, complex hydraulics and difficult-to-control series elastic actuators (SEAs), quasi-direct drive (QDD) actuators combining flat, large-diameter motors with low-backlash, low gear ratios have become the mainstream.
sections.details:
When a legged robot interacts with the environment, landing generates vertical ground reaction forces (GRF) of up to three times its body weight. Actuators therefore demand characteristics opposite to industrial robot arms, which focus on high gear ratios, high stiffness, and precise positioning. Legged joints require high backdrivability—the ability for external forces to push back the joint—and low mechanical impedance to absorb impacts quickly and smoothly.

Historically, three main approaches were explored through trial and error:
- High-ratio electric motors: High friction caused external impact shocks to directly damage gearboxes, making joint torque control exceptionally difficult.
- Series Elastic Actuators (SEA): Springs were placed in series to absorb impacts, but resonance narrowed the control bandwidth, limiting high-speed force control.
- Hydraulic actuators: Boasting very high power-to-weight ratios, they powered early Boston Dynamics robots through astonishing jumps and flips. However, fluid leaks, noise, complex piping, and high maintenance costs hindered commercial adoption.

Quasi-direct drive (QDD) actuators broke through these barriers by pairing pancake brushless DC motors with large gap radii and low-reduction planetary gears (around 10:1). With negligible gear friction, joints can accurately estimate and control torque simply by multiplying motor current by the torque constant and gear ratio, without needing expensive joint torque sensors. Open-source initiatives from Unitree and research institutions (such as MIT Mini Cheetah) accelerated adoption, turning QDD into the de facto standard for modern quadrupeds and new-generation humanoids like ARTEMIS.

Sensors have also undergone dramatic advances. Beyond fusing proprioceptive sensing from joint encoders and IMUs, real-time integration of exteroception via LiDAR and RGB-D cameras now enables robots to predict foothold geometry before touchdown.

sections.heading: The RL revolution: Conquering the wilderness and leaping toward semantic walking
sections.summary: The shift from simplified-model Model Predictive Control (MPC) to end-to-end reinforcement learning using physics simulators and PPO has enabled traversal across unmapped rough terrain. The frontier is now moving beyond geometric foothold detection toward "semantic locomotion" that visually discerns physical ground properties like loose gravel or fallen branches.
sections.details:
Locomotion control typically employs a hierarchy: high-frequency low-level control (actuator torque control at 200–1000 Hz, joint trajectory/locomotion generation at 50–200 Hz) and lower-frequency high-level navigation (below 30 Hz). Traditional Model Predictive Control (MPC) achieved real-time computation using reduced-order models like inverted pendulums, but could not capture all the nonlinearities and uncertainties of real-world contact.

Reinforcement learning in simulation (principally the PPO algorithm) broke through this barrier. Key design choices include:
- Output space: Instead of outputting torques directly, policies predict target joint positions, which low-level PD or impedance controllers convert into torques. This significantly stabilizes exploration during training.
- Bridging the gap: Combining system identification of actuator dynamics, domain randomization across physical parameters like friction and mass, and online domain adaptation learning has enabled zero-shot Sim-to-Real transfer.
- Model architecture: Small MLPs or RNNs with fewer than 10 million parameters are primarily used to ensure millisecond-level real-time inference.

In addition, imitation learning techniques that track human or animal motions from video or motion capture have become established, producing natural, acrobatic gaits without complex manual reward engineering.

The cutting edge is now pursuing "dexterous semantic locomotion." Conventional robots only processed the geometric contours (depth) of terrain. Humans, by contrast, visually assess material properties and affordances—such as slippery wet leaves, crumbling gravel, or breakable branches—and delicately adjust their foot placement and force. Integrating semantic visual information with geometry is beginning to unlock higher-level, more dexterous locomotion.

captions.F2: Figure 2(A) illustrates the Sim-to-Real pipeline where reinforcement learning in simulation transfers zero-shot to physical robots via PD control. Figure 2(B) illustrates the evolutionary stages: from flat ground (proprioception only) to rough terrain (geometric vision), discontinuous terrain, and dexterous semantic locomotion leveraging multimodal vision.

sections.heading: Integrating autonomy and representations: From modular pipelines to foundation models (VLAs)
sections.summary: Legged robot navigation traditionally relied on modular systems loosely coupling odometry, traversability estimation, and global path planning. However, driven by extreme tasks like robot parkour, navigation is being reorganized into unified representations that tightly bind language, vision, and action.
sections.details:
Conventional autonomous navigation systems were built modularly: state estimation, SLAM, traversability estimation, global and local path planning, and locomotion controllers were designed separately with explicit interfaces. A unique advantage of legged robots is leg odometry derived from joint kinematics, which can be fused complementarily with IMUs, LiDAR, and cameras.

However, traditional modular separation faces limitations when judging traversability. Whether terrain is traversable depends not just on slope or step height (geometry), but intimately on the robot's dynamic capability and contact state. Consequently, approaches that evaluate traversability directly by learning forward dynamics without explicit maps, as well as end-to-end RL for high-level navigation, are gaining traction.

The pinnacle of this integration is "robot parkour." When leaping over narrow gaps or clambering over high obstacles, separating navigation (where to go) from locomotion (how to jump) introduces fatal latency. Hierarchical RL operating over latent scene representations has succeeded in coordinating whole-body dynamic motions in real time.

Furthermore, the wave of Large Language Models (LLMs), Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, and Diffusion Policies is reaching legged robotics. Robots are beginning to interpret high-level natural language instructions, maintain semantic spatial memory using 3D scene graphs, and generate actions from few-shot teleoperated demonstrations. Still, architectural questions remain fiercely debated: how to harmonize the millisecond-level real-time control needed for dynamic balance with large foundation models that suffer from significant inference latency.

sections.heading: Data pyramids and flywheels: Overcoming real-world data scarcity
sections.summary: Learning policies for legged robots requires multilayered data, ranging from internet-scale common sense to task-specific proprioceptive logs. While GPU-parallel simulators enable cheap, massive data generation, building a "data flywheel" where real-world data and simulation continuously reinforce each other is essential to capture contact physics and long-tail corner cases.
sections.details:
Collecting data for legged robots is far more challenging than for autonomous vehicles. Instead of structured roads, these robots venture into unstructured environments like dense forests, collapsed ruins, and steep stairways. The resulting data is multimodal, asynchronous time-series information that is deeply tied to robot embodiment (such as leg length and mass distribution).

The paper conceptualizes this through a "scaling data pyramid":
- Base (Web-scale, massive, low cost): World knowledge from general images and text, alongside massive data from rigid-body physics simulations.
- Mid-layer (General robotics data): Offline real-world traversal datasets (such as GrandTour and Sub-T) and human/animal motion capture data.
- Apex (Task-specific, expensive, scarce): Online adaptation data on physical hardware and evaluation data specific to a particular embodiment.

GPU-parallel physics simulators like NVIDIA Isaac Sim have slashed data generation costs by running tens of thousands of robots concurrently. Nevertheless, wide reality gaps persist in domains like leg snagging in dense vegetation, plastic deformation in mud or sand, and high-fidelity RGB rendering.

The key to solving this bottleneck is the "data flywheel." Real-world edge cases (failures) gathered from teleoperation and early deployments are fed back into simulators. Simulators are refined using neural rendering (such as 3D Gaussian Splatting) and learned physics engines. Deploying the upgraded models back to real machines to gather fresh data completes a self-reinforcing loop essential for building robust foundation models.

captions.F4: Figure 4(A) shows the data pyramid representing cost versus specificity of data collection. Figure 4(B) outlines the data flywheel concept, where real deployment, edge-case gathering, simulation improvement, and model training cycle to drive performance.

sections.heading: Legs entering society: From plant inspections to space exploration and entertainment
sections.summary: Quadrupeds have established commercial viability in industrial inspection across oil, gas, and construction sites, and are expanding into agriculture and last-mile delivery. Extreme-environment technologies forged in disaster response challenges (DRC, SubT) are also bearing fruit in lunar/Martian exploration and theme park entertainment robots.
sections.details:
Legged robot applications have shifted decisively from laboratory demonstrations to viable commercial enterprises.

- Industrial Inspection and Patrol:
The biggest commercial success for quadrupeds (such as ANYbotics ANYmal and Boston Dynamics Spot). They autonomously patrol hazardous human environments—offshore oil rigs, mines, substations, nuclear facilities, and construction sites with intricate stairs and scaffolding—monitoring facility health with sensor suites.
- Agriculture, Forestry, and Last-Mile Delivery:
Quadrupeds are used for forest inventorying and orchard monitoring without cellular infrastructure. In urban environments, shared-autonomy and teleoperated systems (such as RIVR) are being piloted for last-mile delivery, ferrying packages from delivery vans to residential doorsteps.
- Defense and Search-and-Rescue:
Tracing their lineage from BigDog's robotic mule concept to the DARPA Subterranean Challenge (SubT), legged robots have demonstrated full autonomous decision-making without tethering or human intervention in signal-denied underground caves and collapsed structures, proving their real-world utility.
- Space Exploration and Scientific Surveys:
Space agencies like ESA and NASA are developing legged robots to explore steep crater slopes and lava tubes inaccessible to wheeled rovers. They are also valued as low-impact tools for ecological wildlife monitoring and non-destructive soil sampling.
- Art and Entertainment:
From early AIBO and RoboCup to Disney's recent bipedal character robots charming theme park guests, expressive dynamic gestures are opening up new value in natural human-robot interaction.

captions.F5: Showcase of legged robots active in the real world: (A) Digit performing logistics delivery and the new electric Atlas handling industrial manipulation; (B) Spot and ANYmal inspecting construction sites and plants; (C) rugged exploration in mountain, underground, and disaster environments; (D) space and scientific exploration; (E) entertainment robots performing soccer and dance routines.

sections.heading: Economic impact and policy: When the automation wave hits the service sector
sections.summary: As legged robots become more affordable (entry-level units dropping to thousands of dollars), automation's impact may spread from manufacturing (about 7.5% of workers) to the broader service industry (around 80%). To protect safety and employment without stifling innovation, tiered regulation based on capability and proactive industrial policies are needed.
sections.details:
Historically, industrial robots primarily affected manufacturing, which accounts for roughly 7.5% of employment in developed economies. However, because legged robots can walk in human environments and manipulate tools, tasks across the service sector and domestic spaces—employing around 80% of the workforce—are entering the scope of automation.

Currently, commercial quadrupeds range between $30,000 and $90,000. Yet rapid commoditization is underway, with compact quadrupeds starting from $2,700 and humanoids from $4,900 (e.g., Unitree). The market is projected to expand across three phases: locomotion only (inspection/haulage), manipulation integration (factories/domestic chores), and social interaction (caregiving/hospitality).

National strategies also diverge noticeably. While Europe leads with risk-based comprehensive rules under the AI Act, Japan fosters deployment in elder care and manufacturing under Society 5.0, and China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology has set humanoid mass production and global leadership as an explicit national target. With China accounting for more than half of global industrial robot installations and building pricing power via strong domestic supply chains, Western nations are growing wary of technological dependencies.

The paper outlines four policy recommendations for the coming 10 to 15 years:
- Capability-based regulation: Regulatory tiers tied to capabilities—minimal oversight for locomotion-only platforms, but stringent safety certifications for robots with whole-body manipulation or direct human contact.
- International standards and military guardrails: Establishing international safety benchmarks and preventing conversion into lethal autonomous weapons systems (LAWS).
- Strategic industrial policy: Prioritizing research funding, manufacturing infrastructure, and talent development over protective tariffs.
- Proactive workforce transition programs: Anticipating the pace of automation by rapidly reskilling workers for complementary roles, such as remote fleet managers and human-robot team specialists.

sections.heading: Conclusion: The premier platform for grounding intelligence in the physical world
sections.summary: Electromagnetic actuators and reinforcement learning solved quadruped locomotion, shifting the battleground to humanoid mass production. The keys to future breakthroughs lie in dexterous whole-body motion driven by semantic understanding and unified data-driven autonomous architectures, making legged robots the core platform connecting digital AI to reality.
sections.details:
Legged robotics has definitively moved beyond science fiction and fragile laboratory prototypes. Technological convergence on electromagnetic QDD actuators has established commercial hardware reliability for quadrupeds, while humanoid makers worldwide are announcing mass production readiness.

Nevertheless, the path to general-purpose robots remains filled with open challenges. Compared to the robust stability of four legs, bipedal balance is much more precarious. Robots must not only walk flat factory floors, but also negotiate fragile, constrained terrains with precise foot placement while withstanding external disturbances. The next frontier is whole-body dexterity—coordinating locomotion and manipulation simultaneously rather than treating them as separate problems.

Furthermore, designing architectures that acquire real-world intelligence end-to-end from diverse multimodal data, moving away from teleoperation and hand-crafted rule bases, remains an ongoing challenge. Researchers worldwide must figure out how to ground large foundation models—evolving rapidly in digital spaces—into legged physical bodies governed by millisecond physical constraints, keeping technical, ethical, and societal systems in lockstep.

takeaways: Securing high backdrivability through quasi-direct drive (QDD) actuators achieved both impact resistance and high-bandwidth torque control, establishing the de facto hardware standard for modern legged robots.

While GPU-accelerated simulation and PPO reinforcement learning unlocked robust rough-terrain locomotion via Sim-to-Real transfer, the next frontier is dexterous semantic locomotion that visually anticipates terrain traits like slipperiness or fragility.

Autonomous navigation stacks are undergoing a paradigm shift: moving away from modular pipelines (odometry, mapping, planning, locomotion) toward unified, end-to-end control through latent representations, as seen in parkour and VLA models.

As hardware commoditization drives prices down into the thousands of dollars, automation will rapidly spread beyond manufacturing into service sectors that encompass 80% of the workforce, making capability-based regulation and proactive workforce reskilling vital.
limitations: Simulators remain limited in modeling entangled vegetation, plastic soil deformation (mud, loose gravel), and high-fidelity RGB contact dynamics, capping what can be achieved entirely in simulation.

Architectures that cleanly integrate multi-million/billion parameter foundation models (like VLAs) with the deterministic, millisecond-level (hundreds of Hz) real-time control loops required to prevent legged falls have not yet been established.

Rigorous safety verification (such as control barrier functions or reachability analysis) remains exceptionally difficult to implement on learned policies, leaving a significant gap in statistical and deterministic safety guarantees around humans.
